extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians interested in exposition and Bourbaki-style formalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for producing/evaluating Bourbaki's structuralist, axiomatic style of mathematical exposition — i.e., highly abstract, set-theoretic, and logically ordered textbook-style presentations. Focuses on choices of definition, axioms, organization and intended reader capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for abstract thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader (and by implication the intended level of exposition) requires 'a certain familiarity with mathematical reasoning and a certain capacity for abstract thought.' (Bourbaki, 2004, v)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki explicitly warns that the series 'requires no particular knowledge of mathematics on the reader's part, but only a certain familiarity with mathematical reasoning and a certain capacity for abstract thought.' This orients the tone and level: exposition assumes abstract reasoning ability rather than motivating examples or informal intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic and abstract method; proceed from general to particular
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of exposition is 'axiomatic and abstract, and normally proceeds from the general to the particular.' (Bourbaki, 2004, v)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose axioms and abstract formulations first, then derive particular instances. The choice is dictated by the goal to provide a solid foundation for modern mathematics; many general ideas and principles are presented up front even when their utility is not immediately apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global logical organization and acyclicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every statement assumes only those results already discussed in preceding volumes/sections; books indicate their logical relationships so 'the reader will thus be able to satisfy himself of the absence of any vicious circle.' (Bourbaki, 2004, v)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a strictly ordered dependency graph across chapters/volumes. At the start of each book/volume indicate how it depends on others so proofs and definitions do not rely circularly on later material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local logical framework: definitions, axioms, and theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical framework of each chapter consists of the definitions, the axioms, and the theorems of the chapter; 'These are the parts that have mainly to be borne in mind for subsequent use.' (Bourbaki, 2004, vi)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within chapters, explicitly present and isolate definitions and axioms before using them in proofs; treat them as the essential stock for later development and cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained development: define from scratch
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is presupposed; 'Everything is defined from scratch and thereafter, the proofs all depend on notions and theorems already given and proved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for presentations that do not tacitly rely on informal background; ensure that all notions used have prior formal definitions in the text to preserve the strict logical order and avoid hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Austere, terse, and impersonal style (no informal motivations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation is 'extremely dry, severe, austere, unified and terse. There are no images, no informal motivations or descriptions, no explanations of the value of this theorem or that definition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor compressed, formal statements and proofs over motivating remarks, heuristics, or pictorial/intuitive explanations. The emphasis is on clarity, precision and economy of presentation rather than pedagogical asides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony: no unnecessary definitions or results
rubrics_metrics.description: The exposition is 'clean, elegant, and efficient. ... there are no unnecessary definitions, axioms, theorems, lemmas and examples in Bourbaki’s mathematics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strip redundancy: include only those definitions and results that are essential for the development. Strive for minimal hypotheses and avoid superfluous lemmas or examples that do not serve structural purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic use of set-theoretic language and first-order logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki 'decides to use systematically, explicitly and in all cases the language of set theory as expressed in first-order logic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a uniform formal language (set theory / first-order logic) across the work so concepts are stated and manipulated within a single, explicit formal framework rather than ad hoc informal notations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms derived by structural analysis (minimal hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms are the result of a 'structural analysis' of known proofs: identify the properties strictly necessary to obtain a given result and eliminate unnecessary hypotheses to obtain elegant demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing an axiomatic theory, analyze representative proofs to extract the minimal set of properties required; present those as axioms so the theory is maximally general and its scope clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define abstract structures and build isomorphism into definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of structure includes intrinsically the notion of isomorphism: 'the only theorems such a theory ought to be able to prove are precisely those that are invariant under isomorphism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate species of structures so that isomorphic instances satisfy the same theorems; design definitions and inference patterns to enforce invariance under isomorphism and to make structure-transport explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize mathematics by structures rather than classical divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki's decision 'brought with it the necessity of a new arrangement of mathematics’ — replacing classical divisions (analysis, geometry, algebra) with the concept of structure and classification via isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the exposition around abstract kinds of mathematical structure (groups, fields, topological spaces, etc.) and their interrelations and isomorphisms, rather than traditional subject-area boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic method as tool for abstraction, reconstruction and extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiomatic method 'functions to abstract new, original concepts from classical settings, and then to use this to reconstruct and extend these classical results in new directions.' (Cartan/Dieudonné quotations)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use axiomatization not as an end but as a means to identify core properties, unify disparate results, and open paths to generalizations and new theorems across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical from epistemic dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the logical component (formal ordering, foundations) from the epistemic component (the 'living construction' that groups theorems and organizes mathematics into meaningful wholes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure formal rigor and ordering (logical dimension) while also organizing material to reveal conceptual connections and classifications (epistemic dimension): group partial theories and highlight the 'web of theorems.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamathematical clarity about species-of-structure formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bourbaki’s formal definition of a 'species of structure' is metamathematical: a species is given by texts/formulas in a language with canonical set-theoretic interpretation; the formalism should allow statements about isomorphism-invariance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing species of structure, provide clear syntactic/signature-level definitions (sorts, signatures, echelon constructions, interpretations) so that structures and their transports (isomorphisms) are precisely defined and manipulable.
